title: 1 Samuel 6:1–9
context: The LORD’s ark has been in Philistine country seven months, after the capture and the plagues of the preceding chapters. The Philistines call for the priests and the diviners and ask how they should send the ark back to its place. They are told not to send it empty, but to return a trespass offering. That offering is five golden tumors and five golden mice, according to the number of the Philistine lords, because one plague was on them all and on their lords. They are to make images of the tumors and of the mice that mar the land and give glory to the God of Israel, in the hope that he will release his hand. They warn one another not to harden their hearts as Pharaoh and the Egyptians did. The plan is a new cart and two milk cows that have never been yoked, with their calves shut up at home; the ark and the gold jewels are to go in a box beside it, and the cart is to be sent away. If it goes up by the way of its own border to Beth Shemesh, then the LORD has done this great evil; if not, they will call it chance. Both traditions read the unit as pagans seeking relief under the LORD’s heavy hand. The priests, the diviners, the images, and the test with the cows are pagan practices, not a method Scripture endorses for Israel; God may overrule them, as the next unit will show. The memory of the exodus in verse 6 is shared ground, not a place to import a later debate about hardening.

verses.text: The LORD’s ark was in the country of the Philistines seven months.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD’s ark was in the country of the Philistines seven months.” The stay is dated, and the ark is still named as the LORD’s even in enemy land.

Arminian readers hear a real stretch of time under God’s hand. The months matter; the Philistines have had space to feel the pressure that now forces a decision about sending the ark away.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that it remains “the LORD’s ark” the whole seven months. His claim does not lapse in Philistine country; the time is the period of his hand upon them, already shown in the preceding chapter.

Both traditions take the verse as a dated notice that sets up the return, shared ground at the opening of the chapter.

verses.text: The Philistines called for the priests and the diviners, saying, “What shall we do with the LORD’s ark? Show us how we should send it to its place.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines called for the priests and the diviners, saying, “What shall we do with the LORD’s ark? Show us how we should send it to its place.” They know it is the LORD’s and that it must be sent back.

Arminian readers hear a real question born of distress. They seek a way to return the ark; the appeal to priests and diviners, however, is a pagan recourse, not a model for how Israel is to inquire of God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the question as an admission that the ark must go home, and they too refuse to treat the diviners as a pattern to be copied. God may still govern the outcome of a badly chosen method, which the following verses will put to the test.

Both traditions read the verse as a decision to send the ark back, reached by means the text reports but does not commend as Israel’s method.

verses.text: They said, “If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, don’t send it empty; but by all means return a trespass offering to him. Then you will be healed, and it will be known to you why his hand is not removed from you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They said, “If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, don’t send it empty; but by all means return a trespass offering to him. Then you will be healed, and it will be known to you why his hand is not removed from you.”

Arminian readers hear even these counselors treating guilt and healing as real. They must not send the ark empty; something is owed, and the hand upon them is his. The “trespass offering” is their own way of naming that debt, not a lesson in Israel’s Levitical rites being taught here as their liturgy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same recognition: it is the ark of the God of Israel, his hand is on them, and they must not send it empty. The offering they have in mind will be specified in the next verse as images of the plague; it is their religious world, not an ordinance given to them by Moses.

Both traditions take the verse as a pagan attempt to address guilt under God’s hand, reported rather than endorsed as a pattern.

verses.text: Then they said, “What should the trespass offering be which we shall return to him?” They said, “Five golden tumors and five golden mice, for the number of the lords of the Philistines; for one plague was on you all, and on your lords.
verses.arminianNotes:
Then they said, “What should the trespass offering be which we shall return to him?” They said, “Five golden tumors and five golden mice, for the number of the lords of the Philistines; for one plague was on you all, and on your lords.”

Arminian readers hear a representative gift, five and five, because the plague was one and the lords were five. The logic is theirs: gold images of the affliction itself. That is sympathetic, pagan offering, not a biblical command to make such images.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the five tumors and five mice as an offering matched to the five lords and to the one plague on all of them. The text states their counsel; it does not stop to bless the method.

Both traditions refuse to turn this verse into a model for worship. The offering is what they devised; the next verses will still call them to give glory to the God of Israel.

verses.text: Therefore you shall make images of your tumors and images of your mice that mar the land; and you shall give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will release his hand from you, from your gods, and from your land.
verses.arminianNotes:
They are to make images of their tumors and of the mice that mar the land, “and you shall give glory to the God of Israel.” “Perhaps he will release his hand from you, from your gods, and from your land.”

Arminian readers hear a true call to give glory, even in a pagan mouth, and a “Perhaps” that is their uncertainty, not a limit on God’s power. The images remain their device; the glory is to go to Israel’s God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that glory is to be given to the God of Israel, and that his hand is confessed to lie on their gods and their land as well as on themselves. The “Perhaps” is the priests’ own tentative hope; it does not make the outcome a matter of chance from God’s side.

Both traditions keep the giving of glory as the right note, and the golden images as a method the text reports without recommending it to the church.

verses.text: Why then do you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? When he had worked wonderfully among them, didn’t they let the people go, and they departed?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Why then do you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts?” When God had worked wonderfully among them, they at last let the people go, and they departed.

Arminian readers hear a warning drawn from the exodus, now spoken by Philistine priests. The lesson they themselves draw is to let the ark go, and not to repeat Pharaoh’s hardness. The verse is a caution from history, not a place to import a later debate about how hearts are hardened.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the comparison with Egypt as the priests’ own argument for sending the ark away. They remember that the LORD had worked wonderfully, and that Egypt finally let Israel go.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground in that memory: hardening the heart against the God who has already shown his hand is folly, and the ark should be allowed to depart.

verses.text: “Now therefore take and prepare yourselves a new cart and two milk cows on which there has come no yoke; and tie the cows to the cart, and bring their calves home from them;
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now therefore take and prepare yourselves a new cart and two milk cows on which there has come no yoke; and tie the cows to the cart, and bring their calves home from them;” The test is carefully stacked: untrained cows, and calves shut away from their mothers.

Arminian readers hear a devised sign, not a command of the LORD. The new cart and the unused cows are their experiment; the next unit will show what God does with it, without turning the experiment into a method Israel is later told to copy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same arrangement as a humanly invented test. Milk cows with no yoke, and calves kept back, would naturally pull against a journey to Beth Shemesh. If the cart goes there, it will not be by easy instinct.

Both traditions take the verse as the setup of a pagan test that God may overrule, not as an approved way of seeking guidance.

verses.text: and take the LORD’s ark and lay it on the cart. Put the jewels of gold, which you return him for a trespass offering, in a box by its side; and send it away, that it may go.
verses.arminianNotes:
They are to take the LORD’s ark and lay it on the cart, put the jewels of gold, the trespass offering, in a box by its side, “and send it away, that it may go.” The ark is to travel with the offering beside it, not as a trophy they still hold.

Arminian readers hear a real letting go. They will not drive the cart; it is to be sent, that it may go. The jewels stay in a box at the ark’s side, a confession that something is being returned.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that the LORD’s ark is laid on the cart and sent, with the gold in a box beside it. The Philistines’ part is to release it; the way it goes will be the question of the next verse.

Both traditions read the sending as the act that puts their test in motion, shared narrative ground.

verses.text: Behold, if it goes up by the way of its own border to Beth Shemesh, then he has done us this great evil; but if not, then we shall know that it is not his hand that struck us. It was a chance that happened to us.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Behold, if it goes up by the way of its own border to Beth Shemesh, then he has done us this great evil; but if not, then we shall know that it is not his hand that struck us. It was a chance that happened to us.”

Arminian readers hear the alternative they themselves name: the LORD’s hand, or chance. Beth Shemesh is treated as the ark’s own border, an Israelite town. The test is theirs; a straight path there will mean he has done this, and the next verses will answer that question by what the cows do.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same fork in their reasoning: either “he has done us this great evil;” or “It was a chance that happened to us.” The following unit will not leave the question open, but the method remains a pagan test, not a promised oracle.

Both traditions take the verse as the sign they proposed, and they wait on the event. God may answer in the cows’ path without endorsing divination as a way of knowing his will.
